candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the XML document parsed by the filter XML parser (the "filter+xml" input filter stream / XMLParserFactory consumers, e.g. import or conversion flows). The parameter type attribute value (default attribute name "t", see XMLConfiguration.DEFAULT_ATT_PARAMETER_TYPE = "t") is concatenated into Class.forName with initialize=true, so the attacker chooses which class is loaded/initialized. The child XML under the parameter element is then parsed by XStream, where nested type information (e.g. the XStream class attribute) lets the attacker pick concrete classes to instantiate.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The type attribute is part of the intended wire format: DefaultXMLSerializer writes it for Object-typed parameters (DefaultXMLParser counterpart, DefaultXMLSerializer lines ~339-342), so the behavior is by design for trusted producers. No in-repo caller was found that directly passes end-user HTTP data; the library's exposure depends on consumers in xwiki-platform (XAR/import/filter conversion flows) that are outside this snapshot. No parameterised-type/allowlist check exists in the parser or XStreamParameterManager, and ParameterXStream does not call any XStream allowTypes/setupDefaultSecurity method, so no counter-control was found in the source. XStream's own default security framework is version-dependent; the snapshot pins 1.4.17 (pom.xml line 540). No runtime confirmation was possible (no execution, no tests in the snapshot).
candidates.impact: Arbitrary class loading/static initialization chosen by XML input, plus XStream object-graph instantiation and field population of attacker-selected classes. With XStream 1.4.17 (no default type allowlist) this is the classic unsafe-deserialization primitive: known XStream gadget chains can lead to remote code execution in the JVM, and even without a gadget it enables classpath probing, unexpected side effects from static initializers and denial of service (crafted object graphs).
candidates.prerequisites: An application flow that feeds untrusted XML into the filter XML parser (XMLParserFactory / DefaultXMLParserFactory, e.g. via the "filter+xml" input filter stream). XStream 1.4.17 is on the classpath (pom.xml line 540), i.e. a version whose default type-security framework is not active/required. The attack needs a parameter element (default element name "p") inside a block whose filter element declares parameters, or a DOM element reaching setParameter with an Element value.
candidates.root_cause: The generic "filter XML" parser treats an XML attribute (default name "t", XMLConfiguration.DEFAULT_ATT_PARAMETER_TYPE) as a fully qualified Java class name and loads it with Class.forName(..., true, TCCL), then hands that class to XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize, which unmarshals the corresponding XML element with ParameterXStream. ParameterXStream (backed by com.thoughtworks.xstream 1.4.17, pom.xml line 540) is created without any allowlist/deny-all security setup, and XMLTreeUnmarshaller.start uses the attacker-chosen class as the root conversion type; nested XStream "class" attributes can further select concrete types. There is no validation that the type belongs to the filter descriptor's declared parameter types.
candidates.title: Attacker-selected class name and unrestricted XStream deserialization in the filter XML parser
candidates.trace: SAX/StAX parse -> DefaultXMLParser.startElement builds the block and, for parameter elements, a Sax2Dom DOM fragment (lines ~404-418); DefaultXMLParser.setParameter -> (value instanceof Element) -> unserializeParameter (line 337); unserializeParameter reads the type attribute and calls parameterManager.unSerialize(Class.forName(typeString, true, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()), element) (lines 364-369); XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize stores that class as DDEFAULTTYPE_NAME and calls this.xstream.unmarshal(new DomReader(rootElement), null, dataHolder) (lines 109-128); ParameterXStream (lines 42-75) supplies no allowed-type restriction and XStream's mapper resolves nested types from the XML; XMLTreeUnmarshaller.start converts the attacker-selected class as the root object (lines 53-65), instantiating it and populating fields via XStream's reflection provider.
candidates.unverified: Reachability from a remotely exploitable entry point could not be confirmed inside this repository: the callers that feed attacker-controlled XML into XMLParserFactory/DefaultXMLParser live in other repositories/modules. The availability of a working XStream gadget chain in the deployed classpath was not verified, and the exact set of classes accepted as XStream root types was not runtime-tested. The impact is therefore stated as a lead, not a confirmed exploit.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data / unsafe object instantiation (CWE-502, CWE-470)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 1419 files (1181 Java) under the repository root; 1418 files are present in the P1 index (1 file missing from the index; index parse is partial: 13 files fully parsed, ~12.7k unresolved calls, no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution). I reviewed main-source files across xwiki-commons-xml (XMLUtils, HTML cleaner/sanitizer, SVG/MathML/HTML definitions), xwiki-commons-filter (XML parser/serializer/parameter manager, filter stream XML), xwiki-commons-xstream (SafeXStream, SafeReflectionProvider, converters), xwiki-commons-job (JobStatusSerializer/DefaultJobStatusStore), xwiki-commons-extension (serializer, repositories, install/history), xwiki-commons-velocity (engine, RestrictParseLocationEventHandler, SecureIntrospector/Uberspector, VelocityParser via sampling), xwiki-commons-crypto (password KDF, keystore, signer/CMS), classloader, environment, configuration, properties, script-safe wrappers, netflux/websocket, cache/infinispan and the top-level build files. Test sources are not part of the snapshot, and no code was executed or built.
limitations: No build, tests, or runtime execution; all statements are source-level only and no finding is runtime-confirmed.
Consumers that would make the submitted deserialization path remotely reachable (e.g. xwiki-platform import/filter flows) are outside this snapshot, so attacker reachability is inferred, not proven.

The P1 index is partial (13 fully parsed files of 1181 Java files; no data/control flow; 1 source file missing from the index), so unindexed or unresolved call edges may hide additional or stronger evidence.
The snapshot contains no test sources and no git history, so the intended trust model and any later security fix could not be compared.
Dependency-level exploitation (available XStream gadgets in the deployed classpath) could not be validated without executing code or inspecting external artifacts.
Line numbers are repository-relative to this snapshot and may not match upstream revisions.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE via DefaultExtensionSerializer's plain DocumentBuilderFactory when parsing extension descriptors (xwiki-commons-extension-api .../repository/internal/DefaultExtensionSerializer.java lines 207-301)
rejected_leads.reason: The factory/setFeature hardening is indeed absent, but exploitation requires a malicious extension descriptor to be parsed (typically a configured remote repository or an administrator-supplied extension), so remote attacker control within the reviewed code is weak; no in-repo untrusted-input path was proven.

rejected_leads.lead: XStream-based job status/log deserialization through SafeXStream/SafeReflectionProvider/SafeTreeUnmarshaller (xwiki-commons-job JobStatusSerializer, xwiki-commons-xstream, XStreamFileLoggerTail)
rejected_leads.reason: SafeXStream deliberately keeps XStream's type allowlist disabled (TODO comment) and SafeReflectionProvider.newInstance is unrestricted, so the deserialization is broad; however the XML sources are local files created by the server (job status/log storage), and no in-repo path lets a remote user write them, so attacker control is unproven.

rejected_leads.lead: Velocity #parse restriction bypass in RestrictParseLocationEventHandler (xwiki-commons-velocity line 51-58: URI.create(BASE + path).normalize().startsWith(BASE))
rejected_leads.reason: Percent-encoded dot segments are not decoded by URI.normalize, so the check can pass encoded traversal strings, but whether the actual Velocity resource loader decodes them (and thus escapes /templates/) is defined outside this snapshot; unverified and therefore rejected as a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Netflux weaknesses: java.util.Random for user/channel/history keys (Utils.getRandomHexString) and no channel-membership check before relaying MSG (NetfluxEndpoint lines 238-338)
rejected_leads.reason: The endpoint appears to rely on the (secret) channel key for authorization; the predictability of new Random() keys remotely and the confidentiality impact were not demonstrable from source alone. The channel-length check and random keys limit practical exploitation.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded accumulation of partial WebSocket message fragments in AbstractPartialMessageHandler (lines 44-54) and no message-size limit in the Netflux endpoint
rejected_leads.reason: A plausible memory-exhaustion/DoS hardening issue, but it is a robustness gap rather than a demonstrated vulnerability and the servlet container may impose limits; not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE configuration look in XMLUtils.parse (xwiki-commons-xml XMLUtils.java lines 588-613) where DOCTYPE is allowed and the external-entity parameters are set to false
rejected_leads.reason: On verification, external-general-entities/external-parameter-entities/load-external-dtd are set to their 'disabled' values, so external entity expansion is prevented; the misleading constant names/comments do not create an XXE. Not a vulnerability on its own.

Reviewed the allow/deny logic (element allowlists, namespace traversal, URI/no-URI scheme checks, data: URI restrictions, event-handler attributes are absent); no concrete browser-executable bypass was identified from source, so no candidate was raised.

summary: Reviewed the xwiki-commons 14.9-rc-1 source snapshot (1419 files; 1418 indexed, 1 unindexed; no tests present; no build/execution performed). I inspected the XML/XStream, filter, HTML-cleaner/sanitizer, Velocity, crypto, classloader, job/history, websocket/netflux, extension-repository and configuration modules. One candidate is submitted: attacker-controlled type selection plus unrestricted XStream deserialization in the filter XML parser (`DefaultXMLParser` -> `XStreamParameterManager`/`ParameterXStream`, XStream 1.4.17). Other suspicious areas (extension-descriptor XXE, job-status XStream, Velocity #parse path check, Netflux randomness/membership, unbounded WebSocket partial messages) are recorded as unconfirmed rejected leads.
